6-1.title: Coordinating Conjunctions (FANBOYS)
6-1.learn:
HOW TO USE COORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS (FANBOYS)

Coordinating conjunctions connect EQUAL ideas — words, phrases, or whole sentences of the same type. The seven are FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. Each shows a relationship:
- and = adds (peanut butter and jelly)
- but / yet = shows contrast (small but mighty)
- or = shows a choice (tea or coffee)
- so = shows a result (I was tired, so I slept)
- for = shows a reason (I smiled, for I was happy)
- nor = adds a negative (not now nor ever)

Example 1 — Joining words: 'I bought apples and oranges.'
'And' joins two equal nouns.

Example 2 — Joining sentences: 'I studied hard, so I passed the test.'
'So' joins two complete sentences and shows the result.

Example 3 — Choosing the right one: 'I wanted to play, ___ it was raining.' The contrast calls for 'but': 'I wanted to play, but it was raining.'

questions.question: Which word is a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS)?
questions.explanation: 'But' is one of the FANBOYS coordinating conjunctions; the others are subordinating conjunctions.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'I was tired, ___ I went to bed early.'
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: being tired caused going to bed early.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'Do you want tea ___ coffee?'
questions.explanation: 'Or' shows a choice between two options.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'She is small, ___ she is strong.'
questions.explanation: 'But' shows the contrast between being small and being strong.

questions.question: What relationship does 'and' show in 'I packed a sandwich and a drink'?

choices.A: It adds one item to another.

questions.explanation: 'And' adds one equal item to another.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'He didn't call, ___ did he write.'
questions.explanation: 'Nor' continues a negative idea: he didn't call, nor did he write.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a coordinating conjunction to join two COMPLETE sentences?

choices.B: I like pizza, and I eat it often.
choices.D: I like pizza with cheese and sauce.

questions.explanation: Choice B joins two complete sentences ('I like pizza' and 'I eat it often') with 'and.'

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'We hurried to the station, ___ we still missed the train.'
questions.explanation: 'Yet' shows the surprising contrast: they hurried, yet still missed the train.

questions.question: Which conjunction best shows a REASON in 'She smiled, ___ she had won the prize.'?
questions.explanation: 'For' gives the reason she smiled — because she had won.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a FANBOYS word to connect two equal ideas?

choices.A: I wanted to go because it rained.
choices.B: I wanted to go, but it rained.
choices.C: Although I wanted to go it rained.
choices.D: Since I wanted to go it rained.

questions.explanation: 'But' is a coordinating conjunction joining two equal complete sentences; the others use subordinating conjunctions.

questions.question: What does FANBOYS stand for?

choices.A: The seven coordinating conjunctions: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
choices.D: The parts of a complete sentence

questions.explanation: FANBOYS is a memory trick for the seven coordinating conjunctions: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'I like apples ___ bananas.'
questions.explanation: 'And' adds bananas to apples as two equal liked items.

questions.question: Which word is NOT a coordinating conjunction?
questions.explanation: 'When' is a subordinating conjunction; 'yet,' 'so,' and 'nor' are all FANBOYS words.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'The movie was long, ___ it was very exciting.'
questions.explanation: 'But' shows the contrast between being long and being exciting.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'It started to snow, ___ we built a snowman.'
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: the snow led to building a snowman.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'You can walk to school ___ ride the bus.'
questions.explanation: 'Or' shows a choice between walking and riding the bus.

questions.question: In 'red and blue balloons,' what does 'and' join?
questions.explanation: 'And' joins the two equal describing words 'red' and 'blue.'

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'Hurry up, ___ we will be late.'
questions.explanation: 'Or' warns of the alternative result: hurry, or being late will happen.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'I wanted ice cream, ___ the shop was closed.'
questions.explanation: 'But' shows the contrast between wanting ice cream and the shop being closed.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'The dog barked, ___ the cat ran away.'
questions.explanation: 'And' simply adds the second event to the first as two connected actions.

questions.question: Which conjunction shows a RESULT?
questions.explanation: 'So' shows that one thing happens as a result of another.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'I practiced every day, ___ I improved quickly.'
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: practicing every day caused quick improvement.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'She wanted to win, ___ she trained for months.'
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: wanting to win led to months of training.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly joins two complete sentences with a comma plus a FANBOYS word?

choices.A: The sky darkened, and rain began to fall.
choices.C: The sky darkened, rain began to fall.

questions.explanation: 'The sky darkened, and rain began to fall.' joins two complete sentences with a comma and the conjunction 'and.'

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'We can order pizza, ___ we can cook at home.'
questions.explanation: 'Or' shows a choice between ordering pizza and cooking at home.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'The test was difficult, ___ everyone passed.'
questions.explanation: 'Yet' shows the surprising contrast: the test was hard, yet everyone passed.

questions.question: In 'slowly but surely,' what relationship does 'but' show?
questions.explanation: 'But' shows a contrast between 'slowly' and 'surely.'

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'You may have cake ___ pie, but not both.'
questions.explanation: 'Or' shows a choice between cake and pie when only one is allowed.

questions.question: Which sentence uses 'so' correctly to show a result?

choices.A: I was hungry, so I made a sandwich.
choices.B: So I was hungry I made a sandwich.
choices.D: Hungry so I a sandwich made.

questions.explanation: 'I was hungry, so I made a sandwich.' uses 'so' between two complete sentences to show that hunger led to making a sandwich.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'Neither the dog ___ the cat would eat the food.'
questions.explanation: 'Nor' pairs with 'neither' to continue the negative: neither the dog nor the cat would eat.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'He stayed home, ___ he was feeling sick.'
questions.explanation: 'For' gives the reason he stayed home — because he was sick.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a FANBOYS word to join two complete sentences and show CONTRAST?

choices.A: The plan was risky, yet they tried it anyway.
choices.B: The plan was risky and bold.
choices.D: The plan, risky yet bold one.

questions.explanation: 'The plan was risky, yet they tried it anyway.' joins two complete sentences with 'yet,' showing the contrast between a risky plan and trying it anyway.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'She did not give up, ___ did she complain.'
questions.explanation: 'Nor' continues the negative idea: she did not give up, nor did she complain.

questions.question: Which FANBOYS word means almost the same as 'because' when it gives a reason?
questions.explanation: 'For' can show a reason, much like 'because': 'She rested, for she was tired.'

questions.question: Read the sentence: 'The road was icy, ___ the driver slowed down.' Which conjunction shows the RESULT?
questions.explanation: 'So' shows the result: the icy road caused the driver to slow down.

questions.question: Which sentence INCORRECTLY uses a coordinating conjunction?

choices.A: I was cold, so I put on a sweater.
choices.B: She knocked, but no one answered.
choices.C: He was tired, or he kept working all night.
choices.D: We were hungry, and we cooked dinner.

questions.explanation: 'Or' should show a choice, but the sentence needs contrast ('but'): he was tired, but he kept working.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'The hikers were exhausted, ___ they reached the summit.'
questions.explanation: 'Yet' shows the surprising contrast: though exhausted, they still reached the summit.

questions.question: In 'I closed the window, for the wind was cold,' what does 'for' show?
questions.explanation: 'For' gives the reason the window was closed — the cold wind.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'nor'?

choices.A: I do not like spinach, nor I like kale.
choices.B: I like spinach, nor kale too.
choices.C: Nor I like spinach or kale.
choices.D: I do not like spinach, nor do I like kale.

questions.explanation: 'I do not like spinach, nor do I like kale.' correctly uses 'nor' to continue a negative, with the verb 'do' coming before the subject.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'The instructions were unclear, ___ we figured it out together.'
questions.explanation: 'But' shows the contrast between unclear instructions and still figuring it out.

6-2.title: Subordinating Conjunctions
6-2.learn:
HOW TO USE SUBORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS

A SUBORDINATING conjunction starts a DEPENDENT clause and links it to a main idea. Common ones: because, although, since, when, if, while, after, before, unless, until. They show a relationship like time, cause, or contrast.

Example 1 — Cause: 'Because it rained, the game was canceled.'
'Because' shows the cause (the rain) for the result (canceled game).

Example 2 — Contrast: 'Although it rained, we still played.'
'Although' shows a contrast — the rain did not stop the playing.

Example 3 — Time: 'When the bell rang, students left.'
'When' shows the time relationship between the two events.

Remember: the clause starting with a subordinating conjunction CANNOT stand alone ('Because it rained' is incomplete). It must connect to a complete sentence. If that clause comes first, put a comma after it.

questions.question: Which word is a subordinating conjunction?
questions.explanation: 'Because' is a subordinating conjunction that starts a dependent clause; the others are FANBOYS.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: '___ it was cold, we wore coats.'
questions.explanation: 'Because' shows the cause (the cold) for wearing coats.

questions.question: What does a subordinating conjunction do?

choices.B: Starts a dependent clause and links it to a main idea

questions.explanation: A subordinating conjunction begins a dependent clause and connects it to an independent clause.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'We waited ___ the bus arrived.'
questions.explanation: 'Until' shows the time relationship — they waited up to the moment the bus arrived.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: '___ you finish your homework, you can play.'
questions.explanation: 'After' shows that playing happens once the homework is done.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a subordinating conjunction correctly?

choices.A: We stayed inside, so it rained.
choices.B: Since it rained, we stayed inside.
choices.C: It rained and so we stayed inside, although.
choices.D: We stayed inside but it rained.

questions.explanation: 'Since' starts the dependent clause and links it to the main idea, with a comma after the opening clause.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction for a contrast: '___ she was nervous, she gave a great speech.'
questions.explanation: 'Although' shows the contrast between being nervous and giving a great speech.

questions.question: Why is 'Because the power went out' a fragment?

choices.B: 'Because' makes it a dependent clause that can't stand alone.

questions.explanation: The subordinating conjunction 'Because' makes the clause dependent, so it cannot be a complete sentence on its own.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'You will not pass ___ you study.'
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if you do not' — you will not pass if you do not study.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates a subordinating clause that comes first?

choices.A: When the rain stopped we went outside.
choices.B: When the rain stopped, we went outside.
choices.C: When, the rain stopped we went outside.
choices.D: When the rain, stopped we went outside.

questions.explanation: When a dependent clause starts the sentence, a comma follows it before the main clause.

questions.question: Which word is a subordinating conjunction?
questions.explanation: 'Although' starts a dependent clause; the others are FANBOYS coordinating conjunctions.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'I will call you ___ I get home.'
questions.explanation: 'When' shows the time relationship — the call happens at the time of getting home.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'We cheered ___ our team scored.'
questions.explanation: 'When' shows the time the cheering happened — at the moment of scoring.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: '___ the sun came up, the birds began to sing.'
questions.explanation: 'When' shows the time relationship between the sunrise and the birds singing.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'I brushed my teeth ___ I went to bed.'
questions.explanation: 'Before' shows the order in time — brushing happened first, then going to bed.

questions.question: Which word can start a dependent clause?
questions.explanation: 'Since' is a subordinating conjunction that begins a dependent clause.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: '___ you are ready, we can leave.'
questions.explanation: 'If' shows a condition — leaving depends on being ready.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'She read a book ___ she waited for the doctor.'
questions.explanation: 'While' shows the two actions happening at the same time.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'We left the party early ___ we were tired.'
questions.explanation: 'Because' gives the cause for leaving early — being tired.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: '___ I had studied harder, I would have done better.'
questions.explanation: 'If' sets up the condition that would have changed the result.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'He kept practicing ___ he made the team.'
questions.explanation: 'Until' shows he practiced up to the point of making the team.

questions.question: Which conjunction best shows a CAUSE: 'The plants died ___ no one watered them.'?
questions.explanation: 'Because' gives the cause — the lack of water — for the plants dying.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: '___ he is only six, he reads chapter books.'
questions.explanation: 'Although' shows the contrast between his young age and his reading skill.

questions.question: Which sentence has a dependent clause?

choices.C: After the bell rang, students packed their bags.

questions.explanation: 'After the bell rang' is a dependent clause; it cannot stand alone and links to the main idea.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'Wash your hands ___ you eat dinner.'
questions.explanation: 'Before' shows the order — handwashing comes first, then dinner.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'I have loved music ___ I was a little kid.'
questions.explanation: 'Since' shows the time the love of music began and continued from then on.

questions.question: Which sentence uses 'while' to show two things happening at once?

choices.A: While I cooked dinner, my sister set the table.
choices.C: Dinner while I cooked the table.
choices.D: While, I cooked dinner my sister.

questions.explanation: 'While I cooked dinner, my sister set the table.' uses 'while' to show cooking and setting the table happening at the same time.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'We can have a picnic ___ it does not rain.'
questions.explanation: 'If' sets the condition — the picnic depends on no rain.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'The crowd cheered ___ the singer walked onstage.'
questions.explanation: 'When' shows the time relationship — the cheering happened as the singer appeared.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly joins an independent and a dependent clause?

choices.A: We canceled the trip because the flight was full.
choices.B: We canceled the trip, the flight was full.
choices.D: We canceled the trip. Because the flight was full.

questions.explanation: 'We canceled the trip because the flight was full.' joins the main idea with the dependent clause 'because the flight was full' to make a complete complex sentence.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'I will not go to the game ___ my friends come too.'
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not' — going to the game depends on the friends coming.

questions.question: Which sentence is INCORRECTLY punctuated?

choices.A: Although she was tired she finished the race.
choices.B: Although she was tired, she finished the race.
choices.C: She finished the race although she was tired.
choices.D: When the race ended, she rested.

questions.explanation: When a dependent clause comes first, a comma must follow it: 'Although she was tired, she finished the race.'

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: '___ the recipe says, you should bake it for thirty minutes.'
questions.explanation: 'Since' here shows a reason — because the recipe says so, you should bake it that long.

questions.question: Which conjunction shows the BEST contrast: 'The dog is tiny, ___ it barks like a giant.'?
questions.explanation: 'Though' shows the contrast between the dog being tiny and its big bark.

questions.question: Why does 'When the movie ended' need more to be a sentence?

choices.B: 'When' makes it a dependent clause that needs a main idea.
choices.D: It already is a complete sentence.

questions.explanation: The subordinating conjunction 'When' makes the clause dependent, so it must connect to an independent clause.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'We stayed at the beach ___ the sun went down.'
questions.explanation: 'Until' shows they stayed up to the time the sun went down.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a subordinating conjunction to show CAUSE?

choices.A: Since the road was closed, we took a detour.
choices.B: The road was closed, and we took a detour.
choices.C: The road was closed; we took a detour.
choices.D: The road was closed, so we took a detour.

questions.explanation: 'Since' is the subordinating conjunction that shows the cause; the other sentences use FANBOYS or a semicolon.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'You can borrow my bike ___ you return it by five.'
questions.explanation: 'As long as' sets the condition for borrowing the bike — returning it by five.

questions.question: In 'Whenever it snows, school closes,' what does the dependent clause tell us?

choices.B: The time or condition when school closes

questions.explanation: 'Whenever it snows' tells the time or condition under which the main idea — school closing — happens.

questions.question: Choose the best conjunction: 'He apologized ___ he knew he had been rude.'
questions.explanation: 'Because' gives the cause for the apology — he knew he had been rude.

6-3.title: Transition Words
6-3.learn:
HOW TO USE TRANSITION WORDS

Transitions are signal words that guide readers between ideas. They show HOW ideas connect:
- ADDING: also, in addition, furthermore, moreover
- CONTRAST: however, on the other hand, in contrast, nevertheless
- EXAMPLE: for example, for instance, such as
- CAUSE/RESULT: therefore, as a result, consequently
- TIME/ORDER: first, next, then, finally, meanwhile

Example 1 — Contrast: 'I was tired; however, I kept going.'
'However' signals a contrast between being tired and continuing.

Example 2 — Example: 'Many fruits are healthy. For example, apples are full of fiber.'
'For example' introduces a specific example.

Example 3 — Order: 'First, gather your supplies. Next, follow the steps. Finally, check your work.'
These transitions show the order of steps.

Varied transitions make writing flow smoothly. Choose the transition that matches the relationship you mean (adding, contrasting, giving an example, showing a result, or showing order).

questions.question: Which transition word shows CONTRAST?
questions.explanation: 'However' signals a contrast between two ideas.

questions.question: Which transition introduces an EXAMPLE?
questions.explanation: 'For instance' introduces a specific example.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'It was raining. ___, we brought umbrellas.'
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' shows the result: because it was raining, they brought umbrellas.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'I wanted to go to the park. ___, it was closed.'
questions.explanation: 'However' signals the contrast between wanting to go and the park being closed.

questions.question: Which transition word shows you are ADDING another idea?
questions.explanation: 'In addition' signals that you are adding another related idea.

questions.question: Choose the best transition for ORDER: '___, preheat the oven. Then, mix the batter.'
questions.explanation: 'First' signals the first step in a sequence of steps.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'Exercise has many benefits. ___, it strengthens your heart.'
questions.explanation: 'For example' introduces a specific benefit as an example.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a transition word INCORRECTLY for its meaning?

choices.A: I studied hard; therefore, I passed.
choices.B: It was sunny; however, we wore coats anyway.
choices.C: I love apples; however, I also love apples.
choices.D: Finally, we reached the top of the hill.

questions.explanation: 'However' should show contrast, but the two parts are the same idea, so it is used incorrectly.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'The roads were icy. ___, the school closed for the day.'
questions.explanation: 'As a result' shows the closing was caused by the icy roads.

questions.question: Which revision uses a transition to improve flow: 'I was tired. I kept going.'?

choices.A: I was tired. I kept going.
choices.B: I was tired; however, I kept going.
choices.C: I was tired; for example, I kept going.
choices.D: I was tired; first, I kept going.

questions.explanation: 'However' shows the contrast between being tired and continuing, making the writing flow smoothly.

questions.question: Which transition word signals the LAST step in a list?
questions.explanation: 'Finally' signals the last step in a sequence.

questions.question: Which transition word shows a RESULT?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' signals that one idea is the result of another.

questions.question: Which transition word means about the same as 'also'?
questions.explanation: 'In addition' adds another idea, just like 'also.'

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'Mix the dry ingredients. ___, add the eggs.'
questions.explanation: 'Next' signals the following step in a sequence.

questions.question: Which transition word shows CONTRAST?
questions.explanation: 'On the other hand' signals a contrast between two ideas.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'Some pets are easy to care for. ___, goldfish only need feeding and clean water.'
questions.explanation: 'For example' introduces goldfish as a specific example of an easy pet.

questions.question: Which transition word signals you are starting the FIRST step?
questions.explanation: 'First' signals the beginning step in a sequence.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'The cake recipe was simple. ___, it tasted amazing.'
questions.explanation: 'In addition' adds a second positive point about the cake.

questions.question: Which transition word shows TIME or order?
questions.explanation: 'Meanwhile' shows that something happens at the same time, signaling time order.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'I love summer. ___, my brother prefers winter.'
questions.explanation: 'In contrast' highlights the difference between loving summer and preferring winter.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'The team practiced every day. ___, they won the championship.'
questions.explanation: 'As a result' shows the win was caused by all the practice.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'Recycling helps the planet. ___, it saves energy and reduces waste.'
questions.explanation: 'Furthermore' adds more supporting reasons, signaling addition.

questions.question: Which transition fits a CONTRAST: 'The directions looked easy. ___, the project took all day.'?
questions.explanation: 'Nevertheless' signals the contrast between easy directions and a long project.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'She forgot her lunch. ___, her friend shared a sandwich.'
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' shows the result: forgetting lunch led to the friend sharing.

questions.question: Which transition best introduces an example: 'Many sports build teamwork. ___, soccer requires players to pass and support each other.'?
questions.explanation: 'For example' introduces soccer as a specific case of a teamwork sport.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'Wash the vegetables. ___, chop them into small pieces.'
questions.explanation: 'Then' signals the next step in the sequence of preparing vegetables.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a CONTRAST transition correctly?

choices.A: The hike was long; however, the view was worth it.
choices.B: The hike was long; however, the view was long too.
choices.C: The hike was long; for example, the view was worth it.
choices.D: The hike was long; first, the view was worth it.

questions.explanation: 'However' correctly shows the contrast between a long hike and a rewarding view.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'Studying improves grades. ___, it builds good habits.'
questions.explanation: 'Moreover' adds another benefit of studying, signaling addition.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'The bridge was damaged. ___, the city closed it for repairs.'
questions.explanation: 'Consequently' shows the result: the damage led to the city closing the bridge.

questions.question: Which transition word shows that two events happen at the SAME TIME?
questions.explanation: 'Meanwhile' shows two things happening at the same time.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a transition word INCORRECTLY for its meaning?

choices.A: The store was crowded; therefore, we waited in line.
choices.B: It rained all week; for example, the picnic was perfect.
choices.C: She practiced daily; as a result, she improved.
choices.D: First, gather your tools. Next, begin building.

questions.explanation: 'For example' should introduce an example, but a rainy week and a perfect picnic are a contrast, so it is used incorrectly.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'Reading widens your vocabulary. ___, it sharpens your imagination and focus.'
questions.explanation: 'In addition' adds more benefits of reading, signaling addition.

questions.question: Which transition correctly completes a CAUSE-and-RESULT sentence: 'The alarm did not ring. ___, we overslept.'?
questions.explanation: 'As a result' shows oversleeping was caused by the alarm not ringing.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'Solar power is clean and renewable. ___, the panels can be costly to install.'
questions.explanation: 'On the other hand' signals the contrast between solar power's benefits and its cost.

questions.question: Which revision best uses a transition to show ORDER in a paragraph of steps?

choices.A: Gather supplies. Follow the directions. Check your work.
choices.B: First, gather supplies. Next, follow the directions. Finally, check your work.
choices.C: However, gather supplies. Therefore, follow the directions.
choices.D: For example, gather supplies. In contrast, follow the directions.

questions.explanation: 'First,' 'Next,' and 'Finally' clearly show the order of the steps.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'Many animals migrate in winter. ___, some birds fly thousands of miles south.'
questions.explanation: 'For instance' introduces migrating birds as a specific example.

questions.question: Which transition shows a RESULT and fits best: 'He missed three days of school. ___, he had a lot of work to make up.'?
questions.explanation: 'Consequently' shows the make-up work was the result of missing school.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a CONTRAST transition?

choices.A: The plan sounded great; nevertheless, it failed.
choices.B: The plan sounded great; nevertheless, it succeeded easily.
choices.C: The plan sounded great; for example, it failed.
choices.D: The plan sounded great; in addition, it failed.

questions.explanation: 'Nevertheless' correctly signals the contrast between a great-sounding plan and its failure.

questions.question: Choose the best transition: 'The museum had ancient art. ___, it displayed dinosaur bones and old maps.'
questions.explanation: 'In addition' adds more items the museum displayed, signaling addition.

questions.question: Which transition best fits: 'The first plan was too expensive. ___, the team chose a cheaper option.'?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' shows the result: the high cost led the team to choose a cheaper option.
